blocks.content: docker push is the reverse of pull, it uploads a local image to a registry so other machines, teammates, and CI/CD pipelines can pull it back down.
Pushing sends a locally built image up to whatever registry its tag points at. This is the step that actually shares an image beyond your own machine, without it, an image only ever existed locally.

blocks.alt: Push is how a local image becomes shareable

blocks.content: 2. The Tag Has to Match the Target Registry
blocks.text: 2. The Tag Has to Match the Target Registry

blocks.content: Docker uses the tag itself to figure out where to push. A plain myapp:1.0 tag targets Docker Hub, but pushing to a private registry requires re-tagging the image first with that registry's full hostname baked in.

blocks.alt: The registry hostname has to be part of the tag itself

blocks.content:
docker build -t myapp:1.0 .
docker tag myapp:1.0 myregistry.com/team/myapp:1.0
docker push myregistry.com/team/myapp:1.0

code.content:
docker build -t myapp:1.0 .
docker tag myapp:1.0 myregistry.com/team/myapp:1.0
docker push myregistry.com/team/myapp:1.0

codes.bash:
docker build -t myapp:1.0 .
docker tag myapp:1.0 myregistry.com/team/myapp:1.0
docker push myregistry.com/team/myapp:1.0

blocks.content: Just like pulling, pushing is layer-aware: the registry tells the client which layers it already has, and only genuinely new ones get uploaded. This is why pushing a small code change on top of an unchanged base image is usually fast, most of the image is already sitting in the registry.

blocks.alt: Existing layers in the registry are never re-uploaded

blocks.content: You cannot push to a registry you are not authenticated against with write access, docker login has to succeed first. This is the basic access control that keeps random users from overwriting a team's production images.

blocks.alt: Write access is checked before any push succeeds

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A push shares a local image by uploading it to a registry, and only layers the registry does not already have are actually transferred.
The tag itself determines the destination registry, which is why pushing to a private registry always starts with re-tagging first.
